analysis.problem_summary: Find the number of indices where the current height array differs from the expected sorted height array.
analysis.intuition: The expected line ordering is simply the input array sorted in non-decreasing order. By cloning the input array and sorting it, we create the exact target array `expected` and can compare elements index by index.
approach: Create a copy array `res` with the same elements as `heights`.
Sort `res` in non-decreasing order using standard array sorting.
Count and return the number of indices where `heights[i] != res[i]`.
analysis.why_it_works: Sorting the copied array yields the exact target array `expected`. Comparing corresponding elements at each index directly counts the number of out-of-order students.
analysis.key_takeaway: When target order is simply non-decreasing order, cloning and sorting gives a direct O(N log N) baseline solution.
analysis.time_explanation: Copying takes O(N) time, sorting an array of size N takes O(N log N) time, and linear comparison takes O(N) time, leading to an overall O(N log N) runtime.
analysis.space_explanation: An auxiliary array of size N is allocated to store the sorted heights, requiring O(N) additional memory.

analysis.problem_summary: Count mismatching height positions without performing an O(N log N) comparison sort.
analysis.intuition: Since height values are constrained to a small range (1 to 100), we can count the frequency of each height. By consuming heights from smallest to largest in sequence, we can determine what `expected[i]` should be at index `i` on the fly.
approach: Initialize a frequency array `countArray` of size 101 to store the frequency of each height.
Maintain a pointer `currHeight` initialized to 1 to represent the current minimum height available.

Iterate through index `i` from 0 to N - 1: advance `currHeight` until `countArray[currHeight] > 0`, compare `heights[i]` with `currHeight`, increment mismatch count if they differ, and decrement `countArray[currHeight]`.
analysis.why_it_works: The frequency array implicitly represents the sorted order. Consuming counts from lowest to highest height simulates inspecting `expected[i]` without allocating or sorting a full copy of the array.
analysis.key_takeaway: When array values lie in a small bounded range, counting sort allows linear-time processing and avoids full comparison sorting.
analysis.time_explanation: Populating the frequency array takes O(N) time. Iterating through `heights` while advancing `currHeight` up to the max height bound K (100) takes O(N + K) total time.
analysis.space_explanation: The frequency array size is fixed at K = 101, taking O(K) (or O(1) relative to input size N) auxiliary space.
